newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: BMC sees return to profit in 1996.
newsitem.headline: BMC sees return to profit in 1996.

text.p: Portugal's Banco Mello Comercial (BMC) expects to return to profit this year after making a loss of 1.8 billion escudos ($11.8 million) in 1995, the bank's president Vasco de Mello said.

"In the first half we turned a profit of around 154 million escudos and we believe that we will have a positive result at the end of the year, although it won't be a very big profit," he told Reuters in an interview.
"We've embarked on a significant restructuring programme and its effects have been felt throughout 1996," he added.
Vasco de Mello declined to make a forecast for 1997 but said the bank would continue to recover financially.
He said BMC hoped to provide return on equity (ROE) of 15 percent by the end of 1998.
BMC, which has total assets of more than 1.0 trillion escudos, is aiming to expand its activities through internal growth while trimming its staff by an average 200 a year.
"We have to adapt to the new competitive environment and probably won't need so many employees," Vasco de Mello said.
Vasco de Mello said the bank might increase its capital again if it continued to grow significantly but this would not take place before 1998.
"Obviously if our activities continue to grow rapidly the question (of a capital increase) will come up again, maybe not in 1997 but in 1998," he said.
BMC recently raised its capital by 16 billion escudos to 58 billion, which resulted in an increase in the number of shareholders to around 20,000 from 3,400 previously.
"It was our intention to let small shareholders in, not big ones. The Jose de Mello group itself lowered its stake to 51 percent (from around 60 percent)."
Small investors, who are mainly BMC clients, now hold around 25 percent of the bank's share capital.
BMC's other main shareholders are BCP/BPA, U.S. American International Group, Corestates Financial Corp, Union Europeene/UIC and Portuguese businessman Ilidio Pinho.
"We're not considering letting in a foreign shareholder with a stake of above 10 percent," Vasco de Mello said.
